newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-SCIENTISTS SEEKING TEST FOR GROWTH HORMONE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-SCIENTISTS SEEKING TEST FOR GROWTH HORMONE.

text.p: Scientists hope to come up with a method of testing for abuse of growth hormone in sport before the 2000 Sydney Olympics, a medical conference was told on Saturday.
There is no test yet to monitor human growth hormone, which helps build muscle and enables athletes to train harder and recover faster.

International Olympic Committee (IOC) medical chief Alexandre de Merode said earlier this year that anti-doping researchers would meet in Lausanne later this month to pool their knowledge on various banned drugs and hormones.

Thord Rosen, of Gothenburg's Sahlgrenska University Hospital, told a medical conference organised by the International Amateur Swimming Federation (FINA) that few studies had been carried out on growth hormone misuse and none had looked at its effect in combination with drugs such as anabolic steroids.
"It is popular among abusers because it is efficient, has few side-effects and is hard to detect," he said.
"We cannot at present detect growth hormone doping but hopefully we will be (able to) by the time of the Olympics in 2000."
Rosen said four research centres in Sweden, Denmark, Britain and Italy were working together on the "Growth Hormone 2000 Project", initiated by the IOC and the European Union.
He said athletes and body-builders believed an anabolic effect of growth hormone was to increase lean body mass and decrease fat mass.
"It is hard to find any direct scientific effect on muscle or muscle strength," he said. "But if you go into a gym and tell them that they will just laugh at you."
FINA has stepped up its fight against doping abuse in swimming in recent years. It carried out 762 out-of-competition dope tests in 1996 at a cost of $42,000. There were no positive tests.

FINA honorary secretary Gunnar Werner told Reuters the federation expected to maintain the level of testing and more than 200 out-of-competition tests had been carried out so far this year. "So far we have not had any positive cases this year," he said.

In another address to the conference, Priscilla Clarkson of the University of Massachusetts said there was no scientific proof that nutritional supplements, with the exception creatine, did anything to improve athletic performance despite heavy marketing promotion.

Creatine, a muscle fuel occurring naturally in meat and fish, has been developed in tablet form. Creatine supplement was used in training by Britain's 1992 Olympic champions Linford Christie and Sally Gunnell.
"It seems creatine is one of the only nutritional supplements that has been proven effective," Clarkson told the conference.
"But when the supplements come out they are marketed like crazy before anyone has the data. The odds lure with fake science...and we are fighting the glamour."
